abstract: Hampole constructs measures of worker task-level exposure to AI and machine learning across firms and occupations from 2010-2023, finding that tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. The paper develops an economic model distinguishing between direct substitution effects (AI replacing specific tasks) and indirect reallocative effects (workers shifting to new tasks within firms), using university hiring networks as an instrumental variable for causal identification. Two factors shape within-firm employment impacts: mean AI exposure (which depresses demand) and exposure concentration (which enables worker reallocation and partially offsets losses). Despite task-level substitution, overall employment effects remain modest due to productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms, suggesting that AI's job-destroying and job-creating forces partially cancel in the aggregate.
keyFindings: Tasks with greater AI exposure experience declining labor demand from 2010-2023, providing longitudinal evidence of AI-driven task substitution across the pre-GenAI period.
Two offsetting forces shape within-firm employment: mean AI exposure depresses demand, while exposure concentration enables worker reallocation to new tasks, partially offsetting losses.
Despite task-level substitution, overall employment effects remain modest because productivity gains at AI-adopting firms increase total labor demand, partially counterbalancing task displacement.
Causal identification using university hiring networks as an instrumental variable supports the theoretical predictions, strengthening the evidence beyond correlational patterns.

The distinction between direct substitution and indirect reallocation effects provides a framework for understanding why aggregate employment statistics may understate the extent of AI-driven labor market restructuring.
methodology: Empirical analysis using natural language processing to measure AI exposure variation across firms, occupations, and time periods (2010-2023). The study develops an economic model separating substitution from reallocation channels and employs university hiring networks as an instrumental variable for causal identification. The approach combines task-level exposure measurement with firm-level employment outcome data.
qualifiers: The instrumental variable approach using university hiring networks, while creative, relies on specific assumptions about how hiring patterns relate to AI adoption that may not hold universally. The study period (2010-2023) primarily captures pre-GenAI adoption patterns; the dynamics may differ substantially for generative AI. Task-level exposure measures constructed via NLP introduce measurement error. The finding that aggregate effects are modest may change as AI capabilities expand and adoption deepens.
